walkthroughs.body_html:
Religion & Ethics: Normative Ethical Theories (Natural Law, Situation Ethics, Kantian, Utilitarianism) — a core area of A-Level Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Religion & Ethics: Normative Ethical Theories (Natural Law, Situation Ethics, Kantian, Utilitarianism) brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Religion & Ethics: Normative Ethical Theories (Natural Law, Situation Ethics, Kantian, Utilitarianism).

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What does natural law theory base morality on?
options: Natural law is the same thing as the laws of physics.
Natural law means whatever happens in nature is morally right.
Human nature and reason — there are objective purposes (telos) built into humans which reason can discover, generating universal moral precepts.
Situation ethics says rules should always be followed.

mcqs.q: What does utilitarianism say is right action?
options: The action that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number — judged by consequences, not intentions or rules.
Utilitarianism says you should always tell the truth.
Whatever makes you personally happy is the right thing to do.
Natural law is the same thing as the laws of physics.

mcqs.q: What is the central principle of situation ethics?
options: Utilitarianism says you should always tell the truth.
You should do whatever feels right in the moment.
The only intrinsically good thing is agape love; rules can be broken if doing so produces the most loving outcome in the situation.
Situation ethics says rules should always be followed.
